items.followUp: Why is acetic acid classified as a weak acid?

rubric.why: Identifies incomplete ionization in water as the reason HF is weak.
rubric.description: HF ionizes only partially in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that HF does not ionize completely in water.

rubric.why: Links HF's strong bond to its incomplete ionization.
rubric.description: The strong H–F bond resists ionization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating HF's strong bond to its weak acidity.

modelAnswer: HF is a weak acid because it ionizes only partially in water, producing relatively few H⁺ ions.
The strong H–F bond resists breaking, which contributes to this incomplete ionization.

items.followUp: Write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of potassium with hydrogen and chlorine.

rubric.why: Checks the correct balanced reaction of sodium with hydrogen.
rubric.description: Sodium reacts with hydrogen to form sodium hydride.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correctly balanced equation.

rubric.why: Checks the correct balanced reaction of sodium with chlorine.
rubric.description: Sodium reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correctly balanced equation.

modelAnswer: 2Na(s) + H₂(g) → 2NaH(s)
2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s)

items.followUp: State five conclusions drawn from Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: Checks the positive, central nucleus and its very small size.
rubric.description: The atom has a very small, positively charged nucleus at its centre.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a central nucleus and 1 mark for its positive charge or very small size.

rubric.why: Checks the concentration of atomic mass and the mostly empty space in the atom.
rubric.description: Almost all the atom's mass is concentrated in the nucleus; most of the atom is empty space.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each of these conclusions.

rubric.why: Checks the conclusion about electrons surrounding the nucleus.
rubric.description: Electrons revolve around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons move around the nucleus.

modelAnswer: 1. An atom has a tiny, positively charged nucleus at its centre.
2. The nucleus is very small compared with the size of the atom.
3. Almost all the mass of the atom is concentrated in its nucleus.
4. Most of the volume of an atom is empty space.
5. Electrons revolve around the nucleus.

items.followUp: Define a compound and describe two kinds of compounds with examples.

rubric.why: Checks that an element consists of one kind of atom.
rubric.description: An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Checks the metal category and a suitable example.
rubric.description: Metals, such as iron or copper.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming metals and giving an example.

rubric.why: Checks the non-metal category and a suitable example.
rubric.description: Non-metals, such as oxygen or sulfur.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming non-metals and giving an example.

rubric.why: Checks the metalloid category and a suitable example.
rubric.description: Metalloids, such as silicon or boron, have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming metalloids and giving an example.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of only one kind of atom.
Elements are classified as follows:
1. Metals: generally conduct heat and electricity; examples include iron and copper.
2. Non-metals: generally poor conductors; examples include oxygen and sulfur.
3. Metalloids: have some properties of metals and some of non-metals; an example is silicon.

items.followUp: Define a co-ordinate covalent bond and explain its formation in the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺.

rubric.why: Checks the defining feature that one atom supplies both electrons in the shared pair.
rubric.description: A co-ordinate covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons contributed by one atom.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a correct definition including donation of both bonding electrons by one atom.

rubric.why: Checks the example's electron-pair donor.
rubric.description: In the ammonium-ion example, the nitrogen atom in NH₃ donates its lone pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying NH₃ and its nitrogen lone pair as the donor.

rubric.why: Checks formation of the bond and the resulting ion.
rubric.description: NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺, forming NH₄⁺; the donated pair forms the co-ordinate bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the donation to H⁺ and 1 mark for the resulting NH₄⁺ or a clear N→H bond representation.

modelAnswer: A co-ordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by the same atom.
For example, in forming the ammonium ion, NH₃ has a lone pair on nitrogen.
The nitrogen atom donates this lone pair to an H⁺ ion: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺.
The bond formed by this donated pair is a co-ordinate covalent bond, represented as N→H.

items.followUp: Write any four typical properties of liquids.

rubric.why: Checks that gases do not have a fixed shape.
rubric.description: Gases have no definite shape and fill their container.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a gas has no definite shape.

rubric.why: Checks that gases do not have a fixed volume.
rubric.description: Gases have no definite volume.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a gas has no definite volume.

rubric.why: Checks the high compressibility of gases.
rubric.description: Gases are highly compressible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying their high compressibility.

rubric.why: Checks the rapid diffusion of gases.
rubric.description: Gases diffuse rapidly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying rapid diffusion.

modelAnswer: 1. Gases have no definite shape and take the shape of their container.
2. Gases have no definite volume and expand to fill their container.
3. Gases are highly compressible.
4. Gases diffuse rapidly.

items.followUp: Write any four characteristics of a suspension.

rubric.why: Checks the nature of a colloid as a mixture.
rubric.description: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a colloid is heterogeneous.

rubric.why: Checks the typical size range of colloidal particles.
rubric.description: Colloidal particles are about 1–1000 nm in size.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the approximate particle-size range.

rubric.why: Checks the scattering of light by colloidal particles.
rubric.description: Colloids scatter light, showing the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the Tyndall effect or light scattering.

rubric.why: Checks the stability of colloidal particles in the mixture.
rubric.description: Colloidal particles do not settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles remain dispersed and do not settle.

modelAnswer: 1. A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture.
2. Its dispersed particles are approximately 1–1000 nm in size.
3. Colloidal particles scatter light, producing the Tyndall effect.
4. The particles do not settle on standing.

items.followUp: Name any two elements known to people in ancient times.

rubric.why: Checks for one element known in early ages.
rubric.description: Names one element discovered or known in early ages.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example, such as gold, copper or iron.

rubric.why: Checks for a second element known in early ages.
rubric.description: Names a second element discovered or known in early ages.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second valid example.

modelAnswer: Gold and iron are two elements that were known in early ages.
